analysis.one_liner: Taxes bailout-firm bonuses above $50,000 at 50% and puts the money into small business loans.
analysis.headline: The Wall Street Bonus Tax Act, backed by 65 House Democrats, never got a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2010, a year after the government bailed out the biggest banks, Rep. Peter Welch proposed a 50% tax on any 2010 bonus above $50,000 paid to current or former employees of firms that received bailout money under the Trouble Asset Relief Program (TARP) [S2, S3]. The bill directed the money into a trust fund that would pay for direct Small Business Administration loans to small businesses [S2, S3]. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Small Business Committee the day it was introduced [S1, S5]. Neither committee ever held a markup or sent it to the floor, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses, which would gain access to a new SBA direct lending program funded by the bonus tax [S2, S3]. It also would have made highly paid employees of bailed-out banks pay a share back on outsized bonuses, addressing public anger that bailout firms were paying huge bonuses while ordinary taxpayers funded the rescue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses; taxpayers seeking bailout accountability

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on the portion of any 2010 bonus above $50,000 paid to current or former employees of firms that received financial assistance under TARP.
Creates a 'Small Business Trust Fund' and directs the revenue to a Small Business Administration program making loans directly to small business concerns.
The bonus tax reaches former employees too, so bankers who cashed out after the bailout could not avoid it simply by leaving the firm.

analysis.who_pays: Highly compensated current and former employees of firms that received TARP bailout assistance, who would pay 50 cents of every bonus dollar above $50,000 earned in 2010 [S2, S3]. Banks would also face pressure to restructure pay to keep the tax from hitting their staff.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bailed-out banks and their top earners

drawbacks.text: The tax applies only to 2010 bonuses at a narrow set of firms, so it raises limited revenue and firms can avoid it by shifting pay into other forms of compensation or by restructuring their TARP status.
It hits every employee of a bailed-out firm who earns a bonus over $50,000, including rank-and-file workers who had no role in the decisions that caused the financial crisis.
Supporters of the banks argued that sharply taxing compensation could make it harder for recovering financial firms to retain staff while the economy was still fragile.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on a small group — highly paid employees of bailed-out banks — and the benefits flow to small businesses through a new direct lending program. The main weakness is design: a one-year tax on bonuses at a limited set of firms is easy to sidestep and would raise only modest revenue, so its real weight is symbolic — making bailout recipients pay back part of their bonuses — rather than a major transfer either way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, but neither ever held a markup or sent it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 12, 2010, the bill was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Small Business Committee.
It gained 64 cosponsors, all House Democrats, but no further action was ever taken on it.
Neither committee scheduled a markup or vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Highly compensated employees of bailed-out banks kept their full bonuses untouched, and the banks avoided any new tax; small businesses never received the new direct lending program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bailed-out banks and their highly paid staff

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wall Street Bonus Tax Act to tax large bonuses at TARP recipient firms and fund small business loans.

for.name: 64 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee Chair Sander Levin
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the tax
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill during the two years it was before his committee.

against.name: Financial firms that received TARP assistance
against.role: Banks and their executives subject to the proposed bonus tax
against.what_they_did: Opposed and lobbied against taxing bailout-era bonuses; the bill never advanced out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no party split was ever recorded; all 65 supporters (the sponsor and 64 cosponsors) were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have taken 50% of every bonus above $50,000 paid in 2010 to current or former employees of TARP-assisted firms, directly cutting into the compensation practices that drew public anger after the bailouts.
The bill created a Small Business Trust Fund and a new SBA program to make loans directly to small businesses, funded by the bonus tax revenue.
